```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H")

```
```{r data, include=FALSE}
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%
```
```{r data split, include=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]
```
```{r grow tree, include=FALSE}
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)
```
```{r tune tree, include=FALSE}
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]
```
```{r prune tree, include=FALSE}
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %
```
```{r predictions test set, include=FALSE}
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")

conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

sensitivity <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # churners detected
specificity <- conf_matrix["No", "No"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "No"])   # stayers cleared
sensitivity; specificity

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

```

# 1. Introduction

Since acquiring a new customer costs more than retaining an existing one, and customers become more profitable the longer they stay (Gupta et al., 2006), it is in a company's best interest to minimise churn, i.e. customers ending their contract and switching to a competitor. This report therefore investigates the churn behaviour of `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` customers of a telecom provider to gain insight into the factors that play a role in their decision to leave, addressing the question: **which customer characteristics are related to churn, and which customers should a telecom provider target to reduce it?**

# 2. Data

The data were provided by a telecom provider and contain `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` customers. For each customer, the data contain *Churn* (yes/no; `r format(sum(data$Churn == "Yes"), big.mark = ",")` customers or `r pct(churn_rate)` churned) and twelve predictors without missing values: the contract term (*Contract*; `r pct(mean(data$Contract == "Month-to-month"))` month-to-month), months with the company (*tenure*; median `r median(data$tenure)`), the monthly and total amount charged (*MonthlyCharges*, median \$`r round(median(data$MonthlyCharges))`; *TotalCharges*), whether the customer has a partner, phone service or multiple lines, the internet provider (*InternetService*: DSL, fibre optic or none) and four add-ons (online security, online backup, device protection, tech support). Churn differs strongly between groups: `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$Contract == "Month-to-month"] == "Yes"))` of month-to-month customers churned against `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$Contract == "Two year"] == "Yes"))` of two-year customers, and `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$InternetService == "Fiber optic"] == "Yes"))` of fibre customers against `r pct(mean(data$Churn[data$InternetService == "DSL"] == "Yes"))` of DSL customers. The data are randomly split into a training set of `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` (70%) and a test set of `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` customers (30%), stratified by *Churn* so that both sets have exactly the same churn rate of `r pct(mean(test$Churn == "Yes"))`. Always predicting "no churn" therefore gives a baseline accuracy of `r pct(acc_baseline)`.

# 3. Methods

To identify which characteristics are related to churn, a classification tree is used. It predicts a categorical outcome by asking a sequence of yes/no questions, such as "is $X_1$ below 10?". Each question splits the observations into two more homogeneous groups, and the final groups (*leaves*) predict their most common class. This yields easy-to-read if-then rules (James et al., 2013). Let $Y$ be a categorical response with $K$ classes and $X_1, \dots, X_p$ the $p$ predictors. The tree is built and assessed in five steps.

*First*, the tree is grown on a training set by *recursive binary splitting* (CART; Breiman et al., 1984). At each node $m$, every predictor $X_j$ and cut-point $s$ is tried, splitting the node into $\{X_j < s\}$ and $\{X_j \geq s\}$, and the split with the lowest weighted Gini impurity of the two new nodes is chosen, where
$$G_m = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk}^2$$
and $\hat p_{mk}$ is the proportion of training observations in node $m$ that belong to class $k$. $G_m = 0$ for a pure node, and $\hat p_{mk}$ is the predicted probability of class $k$.

*Second*, because a fully grown tree also fits noise (overfitting), it is *pruned* to the subtree $T$ that minimises
$$R_{cp}(T) = R(T) + cp \cdot |T| \cdot R(T_0),$$
where $R(T)$ is the share of misclassified training observations, $|T|$ the number of leaves of $T$, $R(T_0)$ the misclassification rate of the tree without splits, and $cp \geq 0$ the **complexity parameter**. A split is only kept if it lowers the relative error by at least $cp$, so a larger $cp$ gives a smaller tree.

*Third*, $cp$ is chosen by **$K_f$-fold cross-validation**: the training set is divided into $K_f$ parts, and the tree is fitted on $K_f - 1$ parts and tested on the remaining part, each part in turn. This gives a *cross-validated error* with its standard error; lower is better. The **one-standard-error rule** selects the smallest tree whose cross-validated error lies within one standard error of the minimum (Hastie et al., 2009).

*Fourth*, the selected tree is evaluated on a separate test set by its **accuracy** (share of correct predictions), **sensitivity** (share of actual positives predicted positive) and **specificity** (share of actual negatives predicted negative). Higher is better, and the accuracy should clearly exceed the **baseline accuracy** of always predicting the most common class. *Finally*, a predictor's **variable importance** is its share of the total Gini reduction over all (also surrogate) splits; higher means more influential.

# 4. Results

The full tree has `r max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])` splits; the cross-validated error is lowest (`r sprintf("%.3f", row_min["xerror"])`) at `r row_min["nsplit"]` splits (Appendix A, Table A1). The one-standard-error rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp_1se)`, a tree with `r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"]` splits and `r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"] + 1` leaves (Figure 1).

```{r tree plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.4, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Pruned tree (per node: predicted class, churn probability, share of training customers)."}
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
```

The tree first splits on contract type, the most important variable (`r var_importance["Contract"]`% of importance), followed by *tenure* (`r var_importance["tenure"]`%) and *TotalCharges* (`r var_importance["TotalCharges"]`%; Table A2). Customers with a one- or two-year contract (40% of customers) rarely leave: only 10% churn. A long contract creates commitment and switching costs. Among month-to-month customers, the type of internet matters most. **New fibre-optic customers** (month-to-month, less than 16 months with the company) are by far the riskiest group: 18% of customers, of whom 81% churn. Fibre is the most expensive service, and these customers have not yet built up loyalty. Longer-standing fibre customers churn less, unless they pay at least \$95.55 per month (62% churn). For month-to-month DSL or no-internet customers, tenure is decisive: after six months only 28% churn, but 63% of new customers without online backup leave: those using more services seem more attached.

On the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test customers, the tree predicts `r pct(acc_test)` correctly, well above the `r pct(acc_baseline)` baseline. The training accuracy is similar (`r pct(acc_train)`), and the unpruned tree reaches only `r pct(acc_full)`. The tree finds `r pct(sensitivity)` of the churners (sensitivity) and correctly identifies `r pct(specificity)` of the customers who stay (specificity).

# 5. Conclusions and Discussion

Churn mainly depends on how strongly customers are tied to the provider: their contract, tenure, and internet service and its price. The provider should target month-to-month customers in their first year, especially fibre customers, e.g. with discounts for a one- or two-year contract, review its most expensive fibre plans, and encourage new DSL customers to use extra services such as online backup. The analysis could be improved: a lower probability cut-off would find more of the `r pct(1 - sensitivity)` missed churners, a random forest would be more stable, and data on satisfaction or competitor prices could reveal causes.

# Appendix A

**Table A1.** Cost-complexity table of the full tree (selected rows, 10-fold cross-validation). Errors are relative to the root-node error; the 1-SE rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp_1se)` (`r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"]` splits).

```{r cp table}
cp_rows <- cp_table[, "nsplit"] <= 25 | cp_table[, "nsplit"] == max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])
cp_summary <- data.frame(cp = sprintf("%.4f", cp_table[cp_rows, "CP"]),
                         Splits = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"],
                         Leaves = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"] + 1,
                         round(cp_table[cp_rows, c("rel error", "xerror", "xstd")], 3))
names(cp_summary)[4:6] <- c("Training error", "CV error", "CV std. error")
knitr::kable(cp_summary, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
```

**Table A2.** Relative variable importance in the pruned tree (percentage of total; includes surrogate splits).

```{r importance table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(var_importance),
                        `Importance (%)` = var_importance, check.names = FALSE),
             format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Appendix B

The code below reproduces all numbers, tables and figures in this report (R 4.3.3, `rpart` 4.1.23).

\begin{lstlisting}[
basicstyle=\ttfamily\fontsize{6}{6.4}\selectfont,
columns=fullflexible,
breaklines=true,

# 1. Packages: rpart fits CART trees, rpart.plot draws them
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

# 2. Load the data (data frame `data`: 4,000 customers, 13 variables)
setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%

# 3. Stratified 70/30 split: 70% of the churners and 70% of the non-churners go to the
#    training set, so both sets keep the 37.5% churn rate; the seed makes it reproducible
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]                          # 2,800 training customers
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]                         # remaining 1,200 test customers

# 4. Grow the full tree: cp = 0 switches off pruning, xval = 10 stores the
#    10-fold cross-validated error (xerror) for every cp value
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)

# 5. Tune cp with the 1-SE rule: smallest tree whose CV error is within
#    one standard error (xstd) of the minimum CV error
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]

# 6. Prune the full tree back to the chosen cp and compute variable importance
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %

# 7. Predict the test set (majority class of the leaf, cut-off 0.5) and evaluate
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

sensitivity <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # churners detected
specificity <- conf_matrix["No", "No"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "No"])   # stayers cleared
sensitivity; specificity

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

# 8. Figure 1: the pruned tree
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)

# 9. Appendix A: cp table (Table A1) and variable importance (Table A2)
cp_rows <- cp_table[, "nsplit"] <= 25 | cp_table[, "nsplit"] == max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])
cp_summary <- data.frame(cp = sprintf("%.4f", cp_table[cp_rows, "CP"]),
                         Splits = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"],
                         Leaves = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"] + 1,
                         round(cp_table[cp_rows, c("rel error", "xerror", "xstd")], 3))
names(cp_summary)[4:6] <- c("Training error", "CV error", "CV std. error")
knitr::kable(cp_summary, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(var_importance),
                        `Importance (%)` = var_importance, check.names = FALSE),
             format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
\end{lstlisting}
